h: A Spitfire, a Dalí and a room full of floating heads
p: Step into the West Court and you'll find a Spitfire hanging from the ceiling, swooping above the displays below. It's a showstopper for kids and grown-ups alike. Elsewhere, Salvador Dalí's Christ of Saint John of the Cross is one of Kelvingrove's most famous treasures, a dramatic and much-discussed painting that the city bought back in the 1950s.

In the East Court, a cluster of white faces with different expressions, known as the Floating Heads, hangs in mid-air. It's a striking installation that captures every emotion from joy to despair, and it's one of the most photographed spots in the building. Look out too for Sir Roger, an Asian elephant who lived in a travelling menagerie and has been on display here for many years, a firm favourite with Glasgow children.

The grand organ in the Centre Hall is used for regular recitals, and hearing it fill the building with sound is a lovely experience, so look at the timings before you go. The building itself was built for the Glasgow International Exhibition of 1901, and there's a much-loved local myth that it was put together the wrong way round. It wasn't, but locals still enjoy telling the tale.

When you're done inside, Kelvingrove Park leads you up towards the University of Glasgow, with the Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery inside its grounds. Byres Road and Ashton Lane are buzzing with cafés, bars and restaurants, and a walk along the River Kelvin will take you down to the Riverside Museum on the Clyde.
